passage:
"Bhaiya, can you help me with this form?"
"Not now, Abhinav! Can't you see I'm—" Yusuf stopped. He put his phone down. "Sorry. That wasn't about you."
"What's it about, then?"
"My boss said in the meeting that my report looked rushed. In front of everyone. I worked all weekend on it."
"So you're angry at him, not me."
"Exactly." Yusuf stood up. "I'm going to walk round the block for ten minutes. Then I'll help with the form."
"And your boss?"
"Tomorrow I'll ask him for fifteen minutes and show him the weekend's work. Calmly."
Abhinav grinned. "Good. Because I'm not your punching bag."

qa.q: What did Yusuf's boss say about the report?
qa.a: That it looked rushed.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf snap at Abhinav over a form?
qa.a: Yusuf was still stung by his boss calling his weekend's work rushed in front of everyone, and the anger leaked out at home before he noticed it.

qa.q: Which choices turned Yusuf's anger toward a fair conversation?
qa.a: He apologised, named the real source, took a ten-minute walk, and planned a calm talk with his boss to show the work.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel once Yusuf explains?
qa.a: Abhinav probably feels relieved it wasn't about the form and respected enough to hear the truth, while still making clear the snapping wasn't okay 🙂

grounding: A young man stung by his boss snaps at Abhinav at home, stops, names the real source, walks, and plans a fair talk with the boss.

passage:
About a month ago, my team lead read out my code in the stand-up and said, "Did an intern write this?" People laughed. I laughed too.
That evening Hafsa asked if I'd bought bread, and I heard myself say, "Do I have to remember everything in this house?" She went very still.
I went out to the balcony and made myself answer one question: who am I actually angry with? Not Hafsa. The team lead. I wrote three lines in my phone: what he said, how it felt, what I want instead.
Then I went back in and said sorry. The next day I asked the team lead for a one-to-one and told him the public comment stung. He looked surprised, and apologised.
— Nitin

qa.q: What did the team lead say in the stand-up?
qa.a: "Did an intern write this?"

qa.q: Why did Nitin snap at Hafsa about the bread?
qa.a: Nitin was still hurt by the team lead's mocking in front of everyone, and that sting came out at home as sharpness toward Hafsa.

qa.q: What steps helped Nitin aim the anger at the right place?
qa.a: Stepping onto the balcony, asking who the anger was really for, writing three lines, apologising to Hafsa, and then asking the team lead for a one-to-one.

qa.q: What might Hafsa have felt when Nitin snapped about the bread?
qa.a: Hafsa likely felt hurt and confused, since a simple question got a sharp reply, which is why she went so still.

grounding: A young adult looks back on snapping at Hafsa at home after a team lead's jibe, then naming the real source, writing it down and speaking to the team lead.

passage:
Counselling session note: Jagdish, 25, bank officer
Jagdish came in saying he'd "turned into a pressure cooker at home". Last Thursday his branch manager told him, in front of customers, that he was "too slow for this job". That night he shouted at his mother over cold rotis and slammed the door on his younger sister.
In session he named the real source himself: "It's the manager I'm angry at. My family just got the steam." We practised his plan: when he feels that heat at home, he steps out for a ten-minute walk, then writes down what he wants to say to the manager.
He has already apologised at home. Next week he will ask the manager for a private word about giving feedback away from customers.
— Afreen (counsellor)

qa.q: What did the branch manager tell Jagdish in front of customers?
qa.a: That he was "too slow for this job".

qa.q: Why did Jagdish shout at his mother over cold rotis?
qa.a: He was stung by the manager's public remark but couldn't answer back at work, so the anger came out at home, where it felt safer.

qa.q: What plan did Jagdish choose for when the heat rises at home?
qa.a: Step out for a ten-minute walk, then write down what he wants to say to the manager, so the anger goes into a fair conversation instead of at his family.

qa.q: How might Jagdish's younger sister have felt when the door slammed on her?
qa.a: She probably felt confused and shut out, since she hadn't done anything and didn't know about the manager.

grounding: A counsellor's note records a young bank officer naming his manager as the real target of anger he had aimed at his family, and planning a walk, writing and a fair talk.

passage:
Tuesday, late
In the review call today Mr Bhosale said, in front of the whole team, "Chetan, are you even trying?" I said "Noted, sir" and smiled like an idiot.
At home Leela asked why the gas bill was still on the fridge. I heard myself snap, "Can you handle one thing without me?" She went very still. That's when I noticed. I've been sharp all evening: with her, with my brother on the phone, even with the auto driver. None of them said "are you even trying". Bhosale did.
So I told Leela, "Sorry. That was about work, not you." Then I walked twice round the lake till my chest stopped buzzing, came back, and wrote what I'll ask him tomorrow: which deadline he means, and what "trying" should look like.
Chetan

qa.q: What did Mr Bhosale say to Chetan in the review call?
qa.a: In front of the whole team, Mr Bhosale said, "Chetan, are you even trying?"

qa.q: Why did snapping at Leela feel almost natural to Chetan that evening?
qa.a: The sting from the boss had nowhere to go, since Chetan had only smiled and said "Noted, sir"; at home the guard dropped and the anger came out at the nearest safe person.

qa.q: What steps helped Chetan aim the anger at the right place?
qa.a: Chetan apologised to Leela and named work as the source, walked round the lake to settle down, then wrote specific questions for Mr Bhosale about the deadline and what "trying" means.

qa.q: What was that moment like for Leela when she went very still?
qa.a: Leela had asked a simple question about a bill and got a sharp, unfair reply, so she was likely hurt and confused until the apology showed it wasn't about her.

grounding: Shows an adult who notices their sharpness at home, traces it to the boss's remark, apologises, and walks and writes before planning a fair conversation.

passage:
Indu: you ok? you hung up pretty fast 😕
Vaibhav: no. sorry. i was rude about the grocery thing
Vaibhav: that wasn't about you
Indu: what was it about then?
Vaibhav: Kapoor ma'am said in the client meeting that my numbers "looked made up". in front of the client
Vaibhav: i've been angry since 3 and you got the leftovers
Indu: ouch. that's a nasty thing to hear
Indu: want to talk when you're home?
Vaibhav: not yet. walking to the station and back first
Vaibhav: then i'll email her asking for 15 mins tomorrow to go through the numbers together
Indu: sounds right. i'll keep the chai warm ☕
Vaibhav: thank you. and sorry again 🙏

qa.q: What did Kapoor ma'am say about Vaibhav's numbers?
qa.a: She said in the client meeting that the numbers "looked made up".

qa.q: What has Vaibhav realised about where the anger really belongs?
qa.a: Vaibhav writes that the rudeness wasn't about Indu and that Indu got the leftovers of anger from the meeting, which shows the real source has been named.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav's plan get right before replying to the boss?
qa.a: Vaibhav walks first to cool down, then asks for a short meeting to go through the numbers together, turning the anger into a fair conversation instead of more snapping 🙂

qa.q: What might Indu have been thinking before the apology arrived?
qa.a: Indu probably wondered what had gone wrong after the call ended so fast, maybe even worrying about having caused it; the explanation lifts that worry.

grounding: Illustrates an adult who texts an apology for snapping at home, names the manager's remark as the real cause, and walks and writes before a fair conversation.
